representations.name: Ken Thompson
representations.lens: Keep privileged mechanisms narrow, and evaluate a build chain at the level where its behavior can actually be trusted.

primary_sources.title: Reflections on Trusting Trust
primary_sources.evidence_locator: pp. 761–763; compiler/login alteration and self-reproducing bootstrap construction.

primary_sources.title: UNIX Time-Sharing System: UNIX Implementation
primary_sources.evidence_locator: Section I, Introduction; least-common-denominator kernel policy and replaceable user programs.

positions.statement: Source inspection alone cannot establish the behavior of a program when the compiler or its bootstrap path can introduce behavior not present in the apparent source.
positions.scope: Compiler and bootstrap trust for the demonstrated class of self-reproducing compiler alteration.

positions.statement: A build-integrity review must include the compiler and bootstrap path, not only the source being compiled.
positions.scope: Evaluation of trust assumptions in a software build chain.

positions.statement: The resident UNIX kernel should make few policy decisions and provide a least-common-denominator base while user programs remain replaceable.

decision_questions: Which component can alter the resulting artifact while remaining outside the review boundary?
Which policy is irreducibly privileged, and which can remain in replaceable user-space or application code?
What evidence would make the compiler and bootstrap path trustworthy enough for this decision?

counterweights.target_or_position: The trusting-trust construction demonstrates a trust-boundary failure mode; it does not estimate its prevalence in a specific contemporary toolchain or select a complete mitigation.

misuse_risks: Treating the demonstration as proof that every compiled binary is untrustworthy without evaluating the actual supply chain.
Treating a least-common-denominator kernel as a mandate to remove all policy from higher layers.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected sources support a compiler/bootstrap trust lens and a historically bounded UNIX-kernel policy lens. They do not prescribe a modern software-supply-chain control set, service architecture, or general security assurance level.

representations.name: Dennis Ritchie
representations.lens: Preserve portable systems-level leverage through simple implementation contracts, then measure and isolate the cost-bearing path rather than guessing about it.

primary_sources.title: The UNIX Time-sharing System — A Retrospective
primary_sources.evidence_locator: PDF pp. 9–11; implementation language, portability, and performance-tuning discussion.

primary_sources.title: The Development of the C Language
primary_sources.evidence_locator: PDF pp. 1–2 and 11–12; C's systems-programming origin, type checking, and compatibility evolution.

positions.statement: Implementing UNIX in a high-level language created portability and maintainability benefits, while preserving the need to account for its runtime and storage costs.
positions.scope: Historical UNIX implementation and porting decisions.

positions.statement: Performance-sensitive code should be identified from the cost-bearing fraction of the system rather than assumed from the choice of implementation language alone.
positions.scope: Tuning a systems implementation after its dominant costs are known.

positions.statement: Language compatibility and type checking are practical systems contracts whose historical omissions create real migration and correctness costs.
positions.scope: Evolution of C and interfaces compiled across versions or declarations.

decision_questions: What portability or maintenance leverage is gained by this implementation boundary, and what measured cost does it introduce?
Which small fraction of the path is actually responsible for the relevant resource or latency cost?
Which language, ABI, or type assumptions must remain compatible across independently changed components?

counterweights.target_or_position: The selected UNIX and C histories document historical trade-offs; they do not establish that C is appropriate for every system or that source portability substitutes for safety properties.

misuse_risks: Interpreting portability as a requirement to suppress every hardware-specific optimization, including a measured hotspot.
Treating the historical C trade-offs as an endorsement of unchecked assumptions in a new interface.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected sources support a historical systems-language and UNIX implementation lens. They do not prescribe a current language choice, memory-safety strategy, distributed protocol, or benchmark result.

representations.name: Michael Abrash
representations.lens: Treat performance as a whole-system constraint: locate the limiting work, challenge the architecture, and exchange work across time or space only against the actual workload.

primary_sources.title: Michael Abrash's Graphics Programming Black Book
primary_sources.evidence_locator: Chapters 1 and 3; optimization perspective, bottleneck identification, and system-level performance reasoning.

primary_sources.title: Ramblings in Realtime
primary_sources.evidence_locator: PDF pp. 1–2 and 9–10; alternative visibility designs, simplification, and precomputation/caching trade-offs.

positions.statement: When optimization produces increasing complexity without a proportional gain, reconsider the design rather than continuing to tune a frozen approach.
positions.scope: Reported realtime-graphics design practice and architecture selection.

positions.statement: The performance-relevant problem is the workload-dependent limiter, so an optimization must be judged in the complete system rather than by isolated local speed.
positions.scope: Performance engineering for software that interacts with contemporary hardware and workload constraints.

positions.statement: Precomputing or caching a result can be preferable to accelerating its repeated computation when the time, memory, and variability trade-off fits the workload.
positions.scope: Quake visible-surface determination and analogous repeated-computation trade-offs.

decision_questions: What measured limiter governs the user-visible constraint, and is the current optimization targeting it?
Would a different algorithm, representation, or precomputation move work out of the critical path more effectively than micro-tuning?
What memory, build-time, correctness, and worst-case variability costs accompany the proposed cache or precomputation?

counterweights.target_or_position: The selected writings report graphics and realtime practice; a simplification or cache can be unsuitable when its memory, invalidation, startup, or correctness cost dominates the actual workload.

misuse_risks: Using a reported graphics optimization pattern as a substitute for measuring an unrelated workload.
Adding caches or precomputation without an explicit invalidation, memory-capacity, and tail-latency analysis.
representations.evidence_boundary: The book and PDF archive are authored technical writings accessed through third-party hosts. They support the reported performance practices and examples, not universal modern hardware claims or an instruction to emulate an author's style.

representations.name: Brendan Gregg
representations.lens: Diagnose production performance systematically: enumerate resources and failure signals before drilling into workload-specific causality, then use visualization to make sampled evidence inspectable.

primary_sources.title: The USE Method
primary_sources.evidence_locator: PDF pp. 1, 4–6, and 8–9; definition, resource checklist, strategy, and stated limits.

primary_sources.title: Flame Graphs
primary_sources.evidence_locator: PDF pp. 1–5; fixed-rate sampling, stack aggregation, graph construction, and interpretation.

positions.statement: For each relevant resource, check utilization, saturation, and errors before assuming a single bottleneck explains the incident.
positions.scope: Initial server and operating-system performance triage.

positions.statement: A resource-first checklist makes unmeasured areas explicit, allowing a fast initial investigation to distinguish known evidence from known unknowns.
positions.scope: Performance investigations constrained by time or available telemetry.

positions.statement: A flame graph aggregates sampled stack traces so horizontal width represents sample prevalence; it identifies on-CPU hot paths but is not a complete latency analysis.

decision_questions: Which resources have verified utilization, saturation, and error evidence, and which remain unmeasured?
Is the observed problem on-CPU, waiting, or an error/queueing condition that requires a different measurement?
What workload characterization or drill-down would discriminate the first apparent bottleneck from the causal one?

counterweights.target_or_position: Gregg states that USE is one tool in a larger toolbox: it finds bottlenecks and errors efficiently but does not solve every performance problem, and sampled flame graphs describe on-CPU observations.

misuse_risks: Treating a high utilization percentage or wide flame-graph frame as causal proof without saturation, workload, and experiment context.
Running a checklist as a ritual while ignoring absent metrics, measurement interval, sampling bias, or user-visible latency.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works support an operational triage and sampled-profile interpretation method. They do not prescribe a universal SLO, telemetry product, root-cause guarantee, or production remediation.

representations.name: Mike Acton
representations.lens: Design data and transformations around the work the machine performs for the common case, then validate the resulting layout and access pattern against the target hardware and workload.

primary_sources.title: Three Big Lies: Typical Design Failures in Game Programming
primary_sources.evidence_locator: Official GDC session overview and presentation on data-oriented alternatives, hardware costs, and data-over-code design.

primary_sources.title: Data-Oriented Design and C++
primary_sources.evidence_locator: Immutable commit 7b15ec44ac01de0ff3e65a7194b84aca2d4e2366; slides titled Data-Oriented Design Principles and Solve for the most common case first.

positions.statement: Data should be organized around the transformations and access patterns the program actually performs, rather than around a generic object taxonomy alone.
positions.scope: Data-oriented software design for performance-sensitive processing.

positions.statement: The common case should drive the primary design; uncommon cases can be handled explicitly rather than imposing their cost on every operation.
positions.scope: Workload-informed performance design where case frequencies are known or can be measured.

positions.statement: Performance-relevant abstraction decisions need to expose actual data, movement, and access costs to the target machine rather than assuming code structure is the operative unit.
positions.scope: Design review of data layout and processing pipelines on a specified hardware and workload.

decision_questions: What data is touched in the dominant path, in what order, and with what measured frequency?
Which rare cases are currently imposing indirection, branching, allocation, or layout costs on the common case?
What target-machine measurement would show that the proposed layout improves the relevant throughput, latency, or memory constraint?

counterweights.target_or_position: A common-case layout is justified only by the stated workload and hardware constraints; it can be inferior when maintainability, variability, memory use, or a different access pattern dominates.

misuse_risks: Applying data-oriented layout changes before identifying the workload, data volume, and target-machine constraint they are meant to improve.
Treating object-oriented design as categorically invalid rather than selecting the representation that fits the measured work.
representations.evidence_boundary: The official 2010 GDC session and commit-pinned 2014 speaker deck support a data-oriented design lens. The deck is preserved at repository commit 7b15ec44ac01de0ff3e65a7194b84aca2d4e2366; neither source supplies a benchmark result for a different workload.

representations.name: Martin Thompson
representations.lens: For low-latency concurrent paths, remove contended writes through clear ownership and separated coordination, while treating queue, wait, and CPU costs as explicit workload trade-offs.

primary_sources.title: Disruptor: High performance alternative to bounded queues for exchanging data between concurrent threads
primary_sources.evidence_locator: PDF pp. 1–2 and 4–6; contention model, ownership, ring-buffer design, and wait-strategy trade-offs.

primary_sources.title: The Single Writer Principle
primary_sources.evidence_locator: Sections The Single Writer Principle and Impact on Performance; ownership rule and comparative measurements.

positions.statement: If one thread owns writes to a resource, the need for mutual exclusion on those updates can be removed, while visibility to readers still requires an ordering mechanism.
positions.scope: Shared-state concurrency with an ownership model that can assign a single writer.

positions.statement: Concurrent queue costs arise from coordination and contention as well as storage, so separating producer, consumer, and data-storage concerns can change the performance shape.
positions.scope: The described LMAX Java pipeline and comparable concurrent exchange paths.

positions.statement: The single-writer principle is a design rule for reducing contention, not a claim that all work must be serialized; the appropriate partition is determined by the resource and workload.
positions.scope: Architectures that can route updates to one owner per mutable resource.

decision_questions: Which mutable resource has contended writes, and can one owner perform its updates without violating throughput or availability needs?
Are producer coordination, consumer notification, and data storage unnecessarily coupled in the current exchange mechanism?
What CPU, latency, jitter, backpressure, and correctness trade-off does the selected wait or queue strategy make under peak load?

counterweights.target_or_position: The Disruptor paper explicitly treats waiting as a CPU-versus-latency/throughput trade-off and notes that multi-producer coordination reintroduces contention; the cited measurements are configuration-specific.

misuse_risks: Replacing every queue or lock with a busy-spin single-writer design without checking CPU budget, backpressure, failure handling, and fairness.
Generalizing the paper's configuration-specific Java and financial-exchange measurements to a different runtime, topology, or workload.
representations.evidence_boundary: The Disruptor paper is co-authored and reports a specific LMAX design and measurements; the selected sources support the represented ownership and contention lens, not a universal claim that lock-free or ring-buffer designs are always faster or simpler.

rejected_candidates.name: John Carmack
rejected_candidates.reason: Hold on evidence sufficiency only: this bounded lane did not establish the required two stable, independently attributable primary technical sources for a distinct generalizable systems-performance lens. This is not a judgment of technical expertise.

saturation: Stopped at exactly six admitted representations because the bounded decision predicates have distinct coverage across trust boundaries, portable systems implementation, architecture-level optimization, systems triage, data layout, and concurrent ownership. Further expansion would duplicate an admitted lens or require additional qualifying primary evidence; John Carmack remains on hold solely for the latter reason.
